title: Remember the subproblem
summary: Replace a failing greedy choice with bottom-up dynamic programming and identify overlapping subproblems.

scenario.briefing: The vending machine needs the fewest coins for an amount. The current code always takes the largest coin that fits, which is wrong for some denominations. Replace it with a solution that considers every coin and remembers each smaller amount.

objectives.description: Solve coin change with bottom-up dynamic programming.
Identify overlapping subproblems and missing memoization.
Explain optimal substructure and when greedy is safe.

hints: A greedy choice is not automatically optimal.
Define the best answer for every amount from zero to the target.
The answer for amount a uses the answer for a minus a coin.
Fill a table from 0 upward and take the minimum over all coins.

misconceptions.description: Taking the largest coin first for every denomination.
misconceptions.testDescription: Finds the optimum when a greedy choice is wrong.
misconceptions.feedback: With coins 1, 3, and 4, greedy takes 4+1+1 for 6 while 3+3 is better. Dynamic programming compares every choice.
The same smaller amounts are recomputed. Memoize or fill a table so each amount is solved once.

misconceptions.description: Assuming a greedy rule is optimal without a proof or counterexample.
misconceptions.feedback: A greedy rule needs an exchange argument or a counterexample check. Coin systems differ, so the rule is not universal.

sections.title: Optimal substructure
sections.body: The best way to make amount a ends with some coin c, so it contains a best way to make a - c. If the smaller solution were not optimal, replacing it would improve the larger one. That is the structure dynamic programming exploits.

sections.title: Overlap makes caching pay
sections.body: A plain recursion solves the same smaller amounts many times. A table filled from zero upward solves each amount once, turning exponential branching into O(amount × coins) work.

sections.title: Greedy needs its own proof
sections.body: Taking the largest coin works for some currency systems and fails for others. Greedy is a claim about the problem, not a shortcut you can assume. Test a counterexample before trusting it.

steps.title: Fewest coins
steps.prompt: Edit coins.js. fewestCoins(coins, amount) returns the minimum number of coins that sum to amount, or -1 when it is impossible. Use a table from 0 to amount; do not pick the largest coin greedily.
hints: The answer for amount 0 is zero coins.
For each amount, try every coin that fits.
Take one plus the best answer for the remainder.
Mark unreachable amounts and return -1 if the target remains unreachable.

findings.label: The same (row, column) states are computed repeatedly.
Without a cache, the call tree grows exponentially.
A memo table keyed by row and column would solve each state once.
The first-row and first-column base cases are correct for this count.
A greedy choice of the shorter direction is equivalent.

verdicts.label: Block until the overlapping states are memoized

steps.explanation: The recurrence is correct but repeated states make it exponential. Memoization or a bottom-up table keeps the same logic with one solve per state.

steps.title: When to remember
hints: Dynamic programming needs both structure and overlap.
A table trades memory for repeated work.
Greedy is a special case, not a default.
Select substructure, overlap, memoization, and proof for greedy; reject obviousness.

statements.label: An optimal solution must contain optimal solutions to its subproblems.
Memoization pays when the same subproblem appears repeatedly.
A bottom-up table can replace recursion and avoid stack depth.
A greedy rule needs a proof or counterexample check before it is trusted.
The locally best choice is always part of a global optimum.

steps.explanation: Dynamic programming combines optimal substructure with cached overlap. Greedy is safe only when its choice property is proven.
